Abstract
This study explored the eects of an acidic fermentation environment on the quality of cigar tobacco leaves 
using air-cured Dexue 1 tobacco leaves as the raw material. Malic acid was used as a pH regulator and three 
concentrations were screened to identify an optimal level for co-fermentation with 1.5% glucose. The potential 
mechanisms by which acidic fermentation reduces tobacco leaf irritancy were also analyzed. Fermentation under 
acidic conditions led to a more balanced chemical composition and to reduced irritancy. In the T2 (0.8% malic 
acid) and T3 (0.8% malic acid + 1.5% glucose) treatment groups, free nicotine proportion decreased by 37.52% and 
46.98%, respectively, compared to the unfermented treatment (CK). Enzymatic activities of carbon- and nitrogen-
metabolizing enzymes (alpha-amylase, neutral protease), a browning-related enzyme (polyphenol oxidase), and a 
polyphenol synthesis enzyme (phenylalanine ammonia lyase) were signicantly higher in fermented tobacco leaves 
than in unfermented ones. Microbial abundance and diversity were also substantially elevated post-fermentation. 
Dominant bacterial genera included Staphylococcus, Pantoea, Ralstonia, Pseudomonas, and Bacillus. Staphylococcus 
exhibited a signicantly positive correlation with protein and nicotine content, as well as a signicant or highly 
signicant negative correlation with total sugar, amino acids, and NH
3
 content. Metabolomic analysis revealed that 
the primary enriched metabolic pathways were the citrate cycle and phenylalanine metabolism. Staphylococcus 
was positively correlated with acetyl-CoA, isocitrate, and trans-2-hydroxycinnamic acid levels, whereas Bacillus was 
signicantly positively correlated with cis-aconitate and citrate. Under acidic conditions, N exists as NH
4
+
, which is 
more stable and less likely to volatilize during combustion, thus reducing NH
3
 release. Moreover, the proportion of 
free nicotine decreased as pH decreased. Collectively, these factors reduced the irritancy of cigar tobacco leaves 
fermented under acidic conditions.

Introduction
Compared with ue-cured tobacco, cigars are uniquely 
hand-made from tobacco leaves that undergo fermenta-
tion and aging. ey are characterized by a richer and 
sweeter aroma, higher physiological strength, and a dis-
tinct style, and their market is rapidly expanding (Zong et 
al. 2023). After air-curing, cigar tobacco leaves undergo 
a specialized fermentation process that enhances their 
quality and usability. e fermentation of cigar tobacco 
leaves is a process in which microorganisms use nutrients 
of the tobacco leaves themselves to grow, metabolize, and 
transform under suitable conditions. It is an important 
link from agricultural raw materials to cigar products (Li 
et al. 2020a, b). Microorganisms produce small-molecule 
metabolites during fermentation by secreting enzymes 
that break down and employ organic substrates such as 
sugars, proteins, and lipids, thereby supporting their 
own growth and reproduction (Liu et al. 2021). After fer-
mentation, tobacco leaves exhibit obvious alterations in 
terms of physicochemical properties; aroma components 
are increased, sensory quality is improved, and these 
changes ultimately shape the unique stylistic features of 
cigars (Zheng et al. 2022). erefore, fermentation is a 
key step in improving the quality of cigar tobacco leaves 
(Zhou et al. 2020). Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, 
Sphingomonas, Pantomonas, and Methylobacterium are 
the primary bacterial genera involved in the fermentation 
of cigar leaves. For instance, Pseudomonas can degrade 
nicotine during fermentation (Wang et al. 2023a, b); sev-
eral Chryseobacterium strains exhibit protease activity, 
enabling them to hydrolyze proteins and produce amino 
acids (Wang et al. 2024), and Bacillus can break-down 
large molecules such as lignin and carotene by secreting 
relevant enzymes, thus generating small aromatic com-
pounds (Maldonado-Robledo et al. 2003). ese micro-
organisms play important roles in shaping the chemical 
composition, improving the quality, and contributing to 
the formation of benecial substances in cigar tobacco 
leaves.
Addition of organic acids to the culture medium aects 
the microbial utilization of carbon sources. For example, 
a previous study showed that adding moderate amounts 
of organic acids during the fermentation of cassava foli-
age silage signicantly alters the bacterial community 
structure. Using malic or citric acid in combination with 
Lactobacillus plantarum increased the abundance of 
potentially benecial microorganism such as Cellulosi-
microbium, Hyphomicrobium, and Oceanobacillus (Li 
et al. 2020a, b). Lv et al. demonstrated that citric acid 
addition minimizes the loss of dry matter and reduces 
the NH
4
+
N content during the fermentation of Amo-
mum villosum silage. is was achieved by inhibiting the 
growth of harmful bacteria such as Enterobacter, Esche-
richia-Shigella, and Pantoea, thereby improving overall 
fermentation quality (Lv et al. 2020). Furthermore, spray-
ing tobacco leaves with an appropriate concentration of 
glucose or citric acid before curing is reported to help 
reduce irritation and unpleasant odors, such as spiciness 
and bitterness (Blum 2005). ese ndings revealed that 
the addition of organic acids or sugar-based compounds 
can reduce smoke irritancy, while also regulating sensory 
quality.
L-malic acid is a naturally occurring organic acid that 
eectively preserves fruit acidity and is considered to 
have a superior taste compared to citric acid. It is also an 
important organic acid produced during human metab-
olism and serves as a key intermediate in the tricar-
boxylic acid (TCA) cycle. L-malic acid can enhance the 
metabolic activity of related microorganisms by promot-
ing reactions within metabolic pathways and has been 
widely used in the food industry for this reason (Wu et al. 
2022). Preliminary tests showed that fermentation under 
acidic conditions signicantly reduces the irritancy of 
cigar tobacco leaves. As pH represents a critical regula-
tory factor in this process, two specic hypotheses have 
been proposed. First, nicotine forms are closely corre-
lated with pH value, and the proportion of free nicotine 
decreases with a decline in pH. Second, under acidic con-
ditions, nitrogen is primarily stabilized in its protonated 
form (NH
4
 Û), which is more stable and less likely to vola-
tilize as NH during combustion. ese two mechanisms 
are considered the primary contributors to the reduction 
in cigar tobacco leaf irritancy. To explore this, malic acid 
was used as a pH-regulating agent to study how a lower 
fermentation pH aects the physiological characteristics, 
microbial diversity, and metabolite enrichment path-
ways of cigar tobacco leaves. e aim was to elucidate the 
mechanism by which acidic conditions reduce irritancy 
and establish a theoretical foundation for improving the 
quality of cigar fermentation.
Materials and methods
Experimental materials
e experimental materials comprised medium, second-
grade cigar wrapper leaves of uniform quality after air-
curing, with a moisture content of approximately 28%. 
ese were obtained in 2024 from the traditional cigar 
variety Dexue 1 provided by the Sichuan Tobacco Com-
pany (Sichuan, China).
Experimental design
Screening for optimal malic acid concentration
Malic acid was used at concentrations of 0.4%, 0.8%, 
and 1.2%, designated as P1, P2, and P3, respectively. e 
unfermented samples served as the control (CK). After 
moisture regain, 500 g of tobacco leaves was evenly 
sprayed with the respective malic acid solutions, allowed 
to stand for 10min, and then sealed in self-sealing bags.

Fermentation was conducted for 7 d under controlled 
indoor conditions (temperature, 40 ; relative humid-
ity, 80%). Nicotine, protein, total nitrogen, and reducing 
sugar content, as well as sensory quality, were analyzed 
for each treatment. Principal component analysis (PCA) 
was used to determine the optimal concentration of 
malic acid.
Synergistic fermentation of malic acid and glucose
e samples were organized into four treatment groups: 
unfermented (CK), distilled water (T1), 0.8% malic acid 
(T2), and 0.8% malic acid + 1.5% glucose (T3), with three 
replicates per treatment. After moisture regain, 1 kg of 
tobacco leaves per treatment was uniformly spray-misted 
with the respective solutions. Samples were allowed to 
stand for 10 min and then sealed in self-sealing bags. 
Fermentation was performed for 28 d under controlled 
indoor conditions (temperature, 40 ; relative humid-
ity, 80%). After fermentation, 20g of tobacco leaves was 
rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at  80  for 
subsequent enzyme activity, amino acid content, micro-
bial diversity, and metabolomic analyses. A 100g portion 
of tobacco leaves was dried in an oven at 60 °C for 4 h, 
ground, and passed through a 0.25 mm mesh sieve (60 
mesh) for the analysis of conventional chemical compo-
nents and free nicotine content. An additional 200 g of 
tobacco leaves was manually rolled into cigars of uniform 
specications for sensory quality evaluation. For metabo-
lomics determination and sensory quality evaluations, 
six biological replicates were performed per treatment, 
whereas three biological replicates were used for all 
other measurements. erefore, all analytical measure-
ments and sensory quality evaluations were performed 
on subsamples derived from the same batch of fermented 
tobacco leaves, thus ensuring consistency and compara-
bility across all experimental results.
Measurement methods
Chemical composition
Total sugar and reducing sugar contents were determined 
in accordance with YC/T 1592019 using a continuous 
ow analyzer (AA3; BRAN&LU-EBBE, Germany). Pro-
tein content was measured based on YC/T 2492008, 
and total nitrogen content was determined according to 
YC/T 1612002. Nicotine content was determined based 
on YC/T 5592018 using gas chromatography-mass 
spectrometry (GC-MS). e pH of the cigar leaves was 
measured using an acidometer (PB-10; Sartorius, Göt-
tingen, Germany) according to YC/T 2222007. NH
4
+
-N 
content was quantied using the phenol-sodium hypo-
chlorite colorimetric method and a microplate reader 
(Synergy H1; Biotek, Winooski, VT, USA). NH
3
 con-
centration was measured using an ammonia detector 
(EDKORS X-1, China).
Amino acid content
Amino acid content was determined using high-perfor-
mance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Briey, 1 mL 
of ultrapure water was added to 0.05 g of the ground 
tobacco sample in a microcentrifuge tube. After over-
night extraction, the supernatant (200 µL) and an amino 
acid standard solution (200 µL) were transferred to 1.5 
mL tubes. Next, an N-leucine internal standard solution 
(20 µL), triethylamine acetonitrile solution (pH > 7) (200 
µL), and 100% phenyl isothiocyanate acetonitrile solution 
were added and incubated at 25  for 1h. After incuba-
tion, N-Hexane (400 µL) was added, and the solution was 
incubated for an additional 10min. e nal solution was 
ltered and analyzed using a Rigol L3000 HPLC system 
(Beijing, China).
Free nicotine content
One gram of tobacco sample (accurate to 0.0001 g) was 
placed in a 150 mL stoppered conical ask. Subsequently, 
30 mL of CO
2
-free distilled water, adjusted to pH 7.00 
with 0.01 mol/L NaOH, was added. e mixture was 
shaken and extracted at room temperature for 30 min, 
then ltered. Next, 15 mL of the ltrate was transferred 
to a 250 mL separating funnel and extracted twice with 
200 mL of trichloromethane (containing internal stan-
dard n-heptadecane). e organic phases were combined 
for GC analysis. A nicotine standard sample was pre-
pared in a standard solution, and GC analysis was per-
formed to determine the relative retention time of the 
nicotine peak, which was then compared with the relative 
retention time of the corresponding peak in the tobacco 
sample. e internal standard curve method was used 
to quantitatively analyze nicotine content. e GC con-
ditions were as follows: chromatographic column, DB-5 
quartz capillary column; injection port temperature, 250 
; column ow rate, 1.0 mL/min; injection volume, 1.0 
µL; and split ratio, 10:1. e oven temperature program 
was as follows: 100  for 2min, increased at 10 /min 
to 200 , then ramped at 20 /min to 280 , and held 
for 5min.
Enzymatic activity measurements
Tobacco polyphenol oxidase (PPO), phenylalanine 
ammonia lyase (PAL), alpha-amylase (-AL), and neu-
tral protease (NP) activities were measured using reagent 
kits (Suzhou Keming Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Jiangsu, 
China).
Microbial diversity analysis
Microbial DNA was extracted using a HiPure Soil 
DNA Kit (Magen, Guangzhou, China). e V5V7 
region of 16 S rDNA was amplied using the fol-
lowing specic barcoded PCR primers: 799 F 
(5-AACMGGATTAGATACCCKG-3) and 1193R (5- A

C G T C A T C C C C A C C T T C C-3). In addition, the fungal 
amplication primers used were ITS1F (5- C T T G G T C 
A T T T A G A A G T A A-3) and ITS2 (5- G C T G T G T C T T 
A T C G A T G C-3). e target region of ribosomal RNA 
was amplied using PCR. e amplication products 
were quantied using a QuantiFluor uorometer (Pro-
mega, Madison, WI, USA), followed by library construc-
tion and sequencing using an Illumina PE250 platform 
(San Diego, CA, USA). e sequencing data were spliced 
using FLASH (v.1.2.7) (Magoc and Salzberg 2011) to 
obtain raw reads, which were then ltered and processed 
using Fastp software (Bokulich et al. 2013). e Uparse 
algorithm (Edgar 2013) was used for clustering analy-
sis, and sequences were clustered into operational taxo-
nomic units (OTUs) based on 97% similarity. e OTU 
sequences were then annotated and aligned with the spe-
cies. Bacterial OTUs were annotated using the Mothur 
method and the SILVA138 SSU rRNA database. Fungal 
OTUs were annotated and analyzed using the Basic Local 
Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) method in Quantita-
tive Insights Into Microbial Ecology (QIIME) software 
(v.1.9.1) and the Unite (v.8.2) database (Edgar 2004; Wang 
et al. 2007).
Metabolomic analysis
e samples were separated using an Agilent 1290 Inn-
ity LC Ultra (U)HPLC (hydrophilic interaction liquid 
chromatography, HILIC) system (Santa Clara, CA, USA) 
at a column temperature of 25 °C, ow rate of 0.5 mL/
min, and injection volume of 2 µL. Samples were loaded 
onto a Hypersil Gold column (100mm × 2.1mm, 1.9m) 
using a linear gradient deliver over 17min (ow rate: 0.2 
mL/min). For positive polarity mode, 0.1% FA in water 
was used as eluent A, and methanol was used as eluent 
B. For negative polarity mode, 5 mM ammonium acetate 
(pH 9.0) was used as eluent A, and methanol was used 
as eluent B. e solvent gradient program was as follows: 
2% B for 1.5min; 2%100% B over 12.0min; 100% B for 
14.0min; 100%2% B over 14.1min; and 2% B for 17min. 
A Triple TOF 6600 Quantity Spectrometer (AB SCIEX, 
Framingham, MA, USA) was used for high-resolution 
spectrometry. Dierential metabolites between groups 
were screened using orthogonal partial least squares-dis-
criminant analysis (OPLS-DA), based on variable impor-
tance in projection values and P-values from Students 
t-tests. Metabolite levels were considered signicantly 
dierent when the variable importance in projection was 
 1  and P < 0.05. Each treatment was conducted using six 
biological replicates to ensure biological universality and 
reliability of the experimental results.
Sensory quality evaluation
After fermentation, the tobacco leaves were manually 
rolled into single-blend cigar samples with a length of 
90mm and diameter of 9.5mm. ese samples were then 
placed in a constant temperature and humidity chamber 
(Binder KBF 240, Germany), maintained at 18 °C and 
68% relative humidity for 30 d to equilibrate the mois-
ture content. Sensory quality evaluation was conducted 
by a panel of six certied professional sensory panelists 
(men, aged 4050 years), among whom three were from 
the National Research Base of Crop Cultivation Physiol-
ogy and Biochemistry, Henan Agricultural University, 
and three were from Sichuan Tobacco Industry Co., Ltd. 
e panelists performed independent scoring on sensory 
attributes, including aroma quality, aroma quantity, after-
taste, oensive odor, sweetness, irritancy, combustibil-
ity, cigarette ash, in accordance with the YC/T 4152011 
Sensory Evaluation Methods for Tobacco Processing and 
using a nine-point system. For statistical analysis of the 
sensory scores, the mean score of the six panelists was 
rst calculated for each treatment. Subsequently, the 
least signicant dierence test (P < 0.05)  was  conducted 
to determine the signicant dierences in sensory quality 
among the dierent treatments.
Data processing and analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using Excel 2011 
(Microsoft, Redmond, WA, USA). Charts were created 
using Origin 2021 (OriginLab, Northampton, MA, USA), 
and statistical signicance testing (P < 0.05)  was  assessed 
by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by 
Tukeys honestly signicant dierence (HSD) test using 
SPSS 22.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). PCA of the 
selected indicators was conducted using SPSS 22.0. Based 
on the classiedO, bacterial and fungal alpha diversity 
was calculated using QIIME software (Sobs, Ace, Chao, 
Simpson, and Shannon indices) (Caporaso et al. 2010). 
Dierential microbiological clusters and representa-
tive taxa were analyzed using linear discriminant analy-
sis (LDA) eect size (LefSe) with LDA thresholds of 3.5 
for bacteria and 2.5 for fungi (Segata et al. 2011). PCA 
and OPLS-DA were conducted using Rstudio and Ropls 
packages (Wang et al. 2007). Species abundance Circos 
plots were generated using Circos software (Krzywinski 
et al. 2009). e Mantel test was conducted using Omic-
Share Tools, and correlation analysis was performed 
using Cytoscape software.
Results
Selection of optimal malic acid concentration
To determine the optimal malic acid concentration, PCA 
was used to evaluate ten related indicators, including 
chemical composition and sensory quality. e factor 
loadings of the ten indicators on the principal compo-
nents were analyzed, and their eigenvalues and contribu-
tions were calculated (Table S1). e standardized values 
of the original data for the ten selected indicators were

was calculated based on the factor loading matrix. e 
linear equations for the primary principal component 
scores were as follows: Y1 = 0.351 × X10.357 × X20.308

Microbial community diversity
After fermentation, the Shannon and Simpson indices of 
bacterial communities in tobacco leaves increased sig-
nicantly. e Sobs, Chao, and Ace indices for bacteria 
in the T3 treatment group were signicantly higher than 
those in the CK and T1 treatment groups. e Shannon 
and Simpson indices for fungi in the T1 treatment group 
were higher than those in the CK treatment group, but 
the dierences were not statistically signicant. e Sobs, 
Chao, and Ace indices in the T3 treatment group were 
higher than those in the CK and T1 treatment cohorts, 
and slightly higher than those in the T2 treatment group, 
although these dierences were not statistically signi-
cant. Overall, fermentation signicantly improved micro-
bial diversity and richness, with the T3 treatment group 
exhibiting the most signicant eect (Table1).
As sequencing depth increased, the rarefaction curve 
approached a plateau, revealing that sequencing depth 
was sucient and that most microbial taxa were cap-
tured. erefore, further analyses were performed 
(Fig.1A and B).
Signicant separation was observed along the x-axis 
between CK and each treatment group, indicating a sig-
nicant change in the bacterial community structure 
after fermentation. e fungal communities in the T2 
and T3 treatment groups clustered together and were 
distinctly separated from those of the other treatments, 
indicating that these fungal communities were the most 
similar (Fig.1C and D).
Microbial community composition
e top-ve bacterial genera were Staphylococcus, Pan-
toea, Ralstonia, Pseudomonas, and Bacillus, accounting 
for > 50% of the total sequences. e relative abundance 
of Staphylococcus in the CK treatment group was signi-
cantly higher than that in the other treatment groups. T2 
treatment signicantly increased the relative abundance 
of Pseudomonas compared to the T1 and T3 treatments, 
with no signicant dierence from that in the CK group. 
e relative abundance of Bacillus in the T3 treatment 
group was signicantly higher than that in the CK and T1 
treatment groups (Fig.2A). e ve most-abundant fun-
gal genera were Aspergillus, Alternaria, Colletotrichum, 
Diaporthe, and Cladosporium. Among these, Aspergil-
lus dominated the fermentation process, accounting 
for > 50% of the total fungal OTUs. e abundance of 
Aspergillus in the CK and T2 treatment groups was sig-
nicantly higher than that in the T1 treatment group, 
with no signicant dierence compared to that in the T3 
treatment group. Alternaria was signicantly more abun-
dant in the T1 treatment group than in the T2 treatment 
group (Fig.2B).
LEfSe analysis was performed to further identify bac-

In total, 35 dierential bacterial populations (LDA > 3.5)

following markers were identied: CK (Kineococcus and

(Salinimicrobium, Bacillus, Jeotgalicoccus, Varibacu-
lum, Pseudarthrobacter, Ruminolibacter, Fermentimo-
nas, Halomonas, Chryseobacterium, and Cryomorpha) 
(Fig.2C and D). Among the fungi, 29 dierential markers 
(LDA > 2.5) were identied, including ve genera: Mal-
assezia, Erythrobasidium, Rhodotorula, Tilletiopsis, and 
Wallemia (Fig.2E and F).

Discussion
During fermentation, the chemical composition of 
tobacco leaves is closely related to microbial activity. 
After the addition of malic acid, the water-soluble sugar 
content of the tobacco leaves increases, likely owing to 
a pH reduction, which partially inhibits the growth of 
alkaline-favoring microbes, potentially limiting respira-
tion and microbial proliferation (Ye et al. 2023). Malic 
acid is an intermediate product in several metabolic 
pathways, such as the TCA cycle, and it may promote 
bacterial growth by enhancing microbial metabolic activ-
ity through its involvement in key reactions, which is 
consistent with the enrichment of carbohydrate metabo-
lism pathways observed in this study (Skorokhodova et 
al. 2022). Previous studies have shown that co-fermen-
tation with malic acid and glucose reduces impurities in 
tobacco leaves, decreases irritancy, increases sweetness, 
and improves overall sensory quality. ese eects may 
be primarily associated with two mechanisms. First, the 
acidic substances derived from malic acid and its metab-
olites can combine with nicotine to form nicotine salts. 
is converts nicotine from its free-base form to a bound 
state, which may reduce its release into smoke and low-
ering smoke irritancy, while also modulating nicotine 
absorption (Blum 2005). e ndings in our study are

would inhibit the colonization and proliferation by less

pronounced increase in dominant microbes often corre-
sponds to reduced diversity in both bacterial and fungal

and diversity than fungal communities, suggesting that 
bacteria may play a dominant role in the fermentation

relative abundances of Pantoea, Ralstonia, and Bacillus 
increased, indicating that these strains can adapt to the 
fermentation process and the complex chemical environ-
ment of tobacco leaves.
Microorganisms may inuence fermentation indirectly, 
primarily through the expression of functional genes that 
aect the biosynthesis and degradation of key enzymes, 
thereby regulating metabolic processes (Ouyang et al. 
2018; Zhang et al. 2023). Based on the results of corre-
lation analysis and PICRUSt2 functional predictions, 
an association existed between dierent microbial taxa 
and the chemical components of tobacco leaves. Nota-
bly, PICRUSt2 is a predictive tool that infers microbial 
functional potential based on 16S rRNA gene sequence 
data, and its predictions do not reect the actual func-
tional activity of microorganisms; thus, the functional 
associations inferred in this study require further veri-
cation through experiments. Bacillus has been reported 
to synthesize various hydrolases such as glucoamylase 
and protease (Huang et al. 2017). Given the increased 
relative abundance of Bacillus in fermented leaves along-
side decreased protein and elevated amino acid levels, 
we hypothesize that members of this genus may con-
tribute to protein hydrolysis and amino acid accumula-
tion, which could improve the taste characteristics of 
tobacco leaves (Liu et al. 2021). Staphylococcus exhibited 
a signicant or highly signicant positive correlation 
with the contents of protein, nicotine, and ammonium 
nitrogen in cigar tobacco leaves. We speculate that the 
potential reasons may be as follows: Staphylococcus 
can secrete proteases to degrade tobacco leaf proteins, 
thereby obtaining amino acids as nitrogen and energy 
sources to sustain its growth (Zhang et al. 2024); mean-
while, the deamination of amino acids promotes ammo-
nium nitrogen accumulation, and some functional strains 
may mediate nicotine transformation through nicotine 
oxidase to further employ it as a carbon and nitrogen 
source (Yao et al. 2025); Additionally, the high-temper-
ature, micro-oxic conditions during mid-fermentation 
could favor Staphylococcus proliferation and enhance the 
activity of enzymes involved in protein degradation and 
nicotine transformation (Zhang et al. 2024). Notably, this 
correlation likely reects a metabolic association rather 
than a direct causal relationship and may be inuenced 
by factors such as metabolic heterogeneity among strains 
within the genus Staphylococcus and mediation by fer-
mentation environmental factors. e specic mecha-
nism of action requires further clarication through pure 
culture experiments, functional gene verication, and 
other approaches. Aspergillus has been conrmed to be 
involved in sugar and protein degradation, and in the 
synthesis of avor-related compounds in tobacco (Mu 
et al. 2020). Additionally, it can create an air-isolation 
eect and inhibit harmful microorganisms, suggesting 
a positive role in tobacco quality formation. e afore-
mentioned microbial taxa do not act in isolation during 
fermentation; rather, they likely regulate leaf quality syn-
ergistically through complex community interaction net-
works (Gralka et al. 2020; Ma et al. 2021).
During the fermentation process, metabolite-enriched 
pathways were primarily the citrate cycle and phenylala-
nine metabolism. Notably, intermediates of carbohydrate 
metabolism can serve as precursors for the biosynthesis 
of aromatic amino acids (Wang et al. 2023a, b). In addi-
tion, the Maillard reaction involving amino acids and 
reducing sugars constitutes a crucial pathway for the 
formation of aroma-forming substances in tobacco and 
is directly correlated with the sensory quality of tobacco 
leaves (Ren et al. 2023). In the present study, citric acid 
was upregulated in the citrate cycle. We hypothesize 
that this is associated with the catalytic action of citrate 
synthase, a key enzyme that mediates the initial reaction 
of the citrate cycle. Changes in its activity may regulate 
the allocation of carbon ux into the cycle pathway and 
enhance overall metabolic activity (Kumar et al. 2023). 
is hypothesis can be further veried by measuring 
the activities of related metabolic enzymes. e prolif-
eration of most microorganisms relies on the endogenous 
organic substances in tobacco leaves. ese microor-
ganisms likely participate in the degradation of carbon-
containing compounds and proteins during tobacco leaf 
fermentation to maintain their own growth and metabo-
lism, thereby promoting the enrichment of metabolites in 
carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism pathways.

tobacco leaves. Among the treatments, cigar tobacco

Abstract
This study explored the eects of an acidic fermentation environment on the quality of cigar tobacco leaves 
using air-cured Dexue 1 tobacco leaves as the raw material. Malic acid was used as a pH regulator and three 
concentrations were screened to identify an optimal level for co-fermentation with 1.5% glucose. The potential 
mechanisms by which acidic fermentation reduces tobacco leaf irritancy were also analyzed. Fermentation under 
acidic conditions led to a more balanced chemical composition and to reduced irritancy. In the T2 (0.8% malic 
acid) and T3 (0.8% malic acid + 1.5% glucose) treatment groups, free nicotine proportion decreased by 37.52% and 
46.98%, respectively, compared to the unfermented treatment (CK). Enzymatic activities of carbon- and nitrogen-
metabolizing enzymes (alpha-amylase, neutral protease), a browning-related enzyme (polyphenol oxidase), and a 
polyphenol synthesis enzyme (phenylalanine ammonia lyase) were signicantly higher in fermented tobacco leaves 
than in unfermented ones. Microbial abundance and diversity were also substantially elevated post-fermentation. 
Dominant bacterial genera included Staphylococcus, Pantoea, Ralstonia, Pseudomonas, and Bacillus. Staphylococcus 
exhibited a signicantly positive correlation with protein and nicotine content, as well as a signicant or highly 
signicant negative correlation with total sugar, amino acids, and NH
3
 content. Metabolomic analysis revealed that 
the primary enriched metabolic pathways were the citrate cycle and phenylalanine metabolism. Staphylococcus 
was positively correlated with acetyl-CoA, isocitrate, and trans-2-hydroxycinnamic acid levels, whereas Bacillus was 
signicantly positively correlated with cis-aconitate and citrate. Under acidic conditions, N exists as NH
4
+
, which is

Introduction
Compared with ue-cured tobacco, cigars are uniquely 
hand-made from tobacco leaves that undergo fermenta-
tion and aging. ey are characterized by a richer and 
sweeter aroma, higher physiological strength, and a dis-
tinct style, and their market is rapidly expanding (Zong et 
al. 2023). After air-curing, cigar tobacco leaves undergo 
a specialized fermentation process that enhances their 
quality and usability. e fermentation of cigar tobacco 
leaves is a process in which microorganisms use nutrients 
of the tobacco leaves themselves to grow, metabolize, and 
transform under suitable conditions. It is an important 
link from agricultural raw materials to cigar products (Li 
et al. 2020a, b). Microorganisms produce small-molecule 
metabolites during fermentation by secreting enzymes 
that break down and employ organic substrates such as 
sugars, proteins, and lipids, thereby supporting their 
own growth and reproduction (Liu et al. 2021). After fer-
mentation, tobacco leaves exhibit obvious alterations in 
terms of physicochemical properties; aroma components 
are increased, sensory quality is improved, and these 
changes ultimately shape the unique stylistic features of 
cigars (Zheng et al. 2022). erefore, fermentation is a 
key step in improving the quality of cigar tobacco leaves 
(Zhou et al. 2020). Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, 
Sphingomonas, Pantomonas, and Methylobacterium are 
the primary bacterial genera involved in the fermentation 
of cigar leaves. For instance, Pseudomonas can degrade 
nicotine during fermentation (Wang et al. 2023a, b); sev-
eral Chryseobacterium strains exhibit protease activity, 
enabling them to hydrolyze proteins and produce amino 
acids (Wang et al. 2024), and Bacillus can break-down 
large molecules such as lignin and carotene by secreting 
relevant enzymes, thus generating small aromatic com-
pounds (Maldonado-Robledo et al. 2003). ese micro-
organisms play important roles in shaping the chemical 
composition, improving the quality, and contributing to 
the formation of benecial substances in cigar tobacco 
leaves.
Addition of organic acids to the culture medium aects 
the microbial utilization of carbon sources. For example, 
a previous study showed that adding moderate amounts 
of organic acids during the fermentation of cassava foli-
age silage signicantly alters the bacterial community 
structure. Using malic or citric acid in combination with 
Lactobacillus plantarum increased the abundance of 
potentially benecial microorganism such as Cellulosi-
microbium, Hyphomicrobium, and Oceanobacillus (Li 
et al. 2020a, b). Lv et al. demonstrated that citric acid 
addition minimizes the loss of dry matter and reduces 
the NH
4
+
N content during the fermentation of Amo-
mum villosum silage. is was achieved by inhibiting the 
growth of harmful bacteria such as Enterobacter, Esche-
richia-Shigella, and Pantoea, thereby improving overall 
fermentation quality (Lv et al. 2020). Furthermore, spray-
ing tobacco leaves with an appropriate concentration of 
glucose or citric acid before curing is reported to help 
reduce irritation and unpleasant odors, such as spiciness 
and bitterness (Blum 2005). ese ndings revealed that 
the addition of organic acids or sugar-based compounds 
can reduce smoke irritancy, while also regulating sensory 
quality.
L-malic acid is a naturally occurring organic acid that 
eectively preserves fruit acidity and is considered to 
have a superior taste compared to citric acid. It is also an 
important organic acid produced during human metab-
olism and serves as a key intermediate in the tricar-
boxylic acid (TCA) cycle. L-malic acid can enhance the 
metabolic activity of related microorganisms by promot-
ing reactions within metabolic pathways and has been 
widely used in the food industry for this reason (Wu et al. 
2022). Preliminary tests showed that fermentation under 
acidic conditions signicantly reduces the irritancy of 
cigar tobacco leaves. As pH represents a critical regula-
tory factor in this process, two specic hypotheses have 
been proposed. First, nicotine forms are closely corre-
lated with pH value, and the proportion of free nicotine 
decreases with a decline in pH. Second, under acidic con-
ditions, nitrogen is primarily stabilized in its protonated 
form (NH
4

tilize as NH during combustion. ese two mechanisms 
are considered the primary contributors to the reduction 
in cigar tobacco leaf irritancy. To explore this, malic acid 
was used as a pH-regulating agent to study how a lower 
fermentation pH aects the physiological characteristics, 
microbial diversity, and metabolite enrichment path-

mechanism by which acidic conditions reduce irritancy

quality of cigar fermentation.

Discussion
During fermentation, the chemical composition of 
tobacco leaves is closely related to microbial activity. 
After the addition of malic acid, the water-soluble sugar 
content of the tobacco leaves increases, likely owing to 
a pH reduction, which partially inhibits the growth of 
alkaline-favoring microbes, potentially limiting respira-
tion and microbial proliferation (Ye et al. 2023). Malic 
acid is an intermediate product in several metabolic 
pathways, such as the TCA cycle, and it may promote 
bacterial growth by enhancing microbial metabolic activ-
ity through its involvement in key reactions, which is 
consistent with the enrichment of carbohydrate metabo-
lism pathways observed in this study (Skorokhodova et 
al. 2022). Previous studies have shown that co-fermen-
tation with malic acid and glucose reduces impurities in 
tobacco leaves, decreases irritancy, increases sweetness, 
and improves overall sensory quality. ese eects may 
be primarily associated with two mechanisms. First, the 
acidic substances derived from malic acid and its metab-
olites can combine with nicotine to form nicotine salts. 
is converts nicotine from its free-base form to a bound 
state, which may reduce its release into smoke and low-
ering smoke irritancy, while also modulating nicotine 
absorption (Blum 2005). e ndings in our study are

would inhibit the colonization and proliferation by less

pronounced increase in dominant microbes often corre-
sponds to reduced diversity in both bacterial and fungal

and diversity than fungal communities, suggesting that

relative abundances of Pantoea, Ralstonia, and Bacillus 
increased, indicating that these strains can adapt to the

ment of tobacco leaves.
Microorganisms may inuence fermentation indirectly, 
primarily through the expression of functional genes that 
aect the biosynthesis and degradation of key enzymes, 
thereby regulating metabolic processes (Ouyang et al. 
2018; Zhang et al. 2023). Based on the results of corre-
lation analysis and PICRUSt2 functional predictions, 
an association existed between dierent microbial taxa 
and the chemical components of tobacco leaves. Nota-
bly, PICRUSt2 is a predictive tool that infers microbial 
functional potential based on 16S rRNA gene sequence 
data, and its predictions do not reect the actual func-
tional activity of microorganisms; thus, the functional 
associations inferred in this study require further veri-
cation through experiments. Bacillus has been reported 
to synthesize various hydrolases such as glucoamylase 
and protease (Huang et al. 2017). Given the increased 
relative abundance of Bacillus in fermented leaves along-
side decreased protein and elevated amino acid levels, 
we hypothesize that members of this genus may con-
tribute to protein hydrolysis and amino acid accumula-
tion, which could improve the taste characteristics of 
tobacco leaves (Liu et al. 2021). Staphylococcus exhibited 
a signicant or highly signicant positive correlation 
with the contents of protein, nicotine, and ammonium 
nitrogen in cigar tobacco leaves. We speculate that the 
potential reasons may be as follows: Staphylococcus 
can secrete proteases to degrade tobacco leaf proteins, 
thereby obtaining amino acids as nitrogen and energy 
sources to sustain its growth (Zhang et al. 2024); mean-
while, the deamination of amino acids promotes ammo-
nium nitrogen accumulation, and some functional strains 
may mediate nicotine transformation through nicotine 
oxidase to further employ it as a carbon and nitrogen 
source (Yao et al. 2025); Additionally, the high-temper-
ature, micro-oxic conditions during mid-fermentation 
could favor Staphylococcus proliferation and enhance the 
activity of enzymes involved in protein degradation and 
nicotine transformation (Zhang et al. 2024). Notably, this 
correlation likely reects a metabolic association rather 
than a direct causal relationship and may be inuenced 
by factors such as metabolic heterogeneity among strains 
within the genus Staphylococcus and mediation by fer-
mentation environmental factors. e specic mecha-
nism of action requires further clarication through pure 
culture experiments, functional gene verication, and 
other approaches. Aspergillus has been conrmed to be 
involved in sugar and protein degradation, and in the 
synthesis of avor-related compounds in tobacco (Mu 
et al. 2020). Additionally, it can create an air-isolation 
eect and inhibit harmful microorganisms, suggesting 
a positive role in tobacco quality formation. e afore-
mentioned microbial taxa do not act in isolation during 
fermentation; rather, they likely regulate leaf quality syn-
ergistically through complex community interaction net-
works (Gralka et al. 2020; Ma et al. 2021).
During the fermentation process, metabolite-enriched 
pathways were primarily the citrate cycle and phenylala-
nine metabolism. Notably, intermediates of carbohydrate 
metabolism can serve as precursors for the biosynthesis 
of aromatic amino acids (Wang et al. 2023a, b). In addi-
tion, the Maillard reaction involving amino acids and 
reducing sugars constitutes a crucial pathway for the 
formation of aroma-forming substances in tobacco and 
is directly correlated with the sensory quality of tobacco 
leaves (Ren et al. 2023). In the present study, citric acid 
was upregulated in the citrate cycle. We hypothesize 
that this is associated with the catalytic action of citrate 
synthase, a key enzyme that mediates the initial reaction 
of the citrate cycle. Changes in its activity may regulate 
the allocation of carbon ux into the cycle pathway and 
enhance overall metabolic activity (Kumar et al. 2023). 
is hypothesis can be further veried by measuring 
the activities of related metabolic enzymes. e prolif-
eration of most microorganisms relies on the endogenous 
organic substances in tobacco leaves. ese microor-
ganisms likely participate in the degradation of carbon-
containing compounds and proteins during tobacco leaf 
fermentation to maintain their own growth and metabo-
lism, thereby promoting the enrichment of metabolites in 
carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism pathways.

balanced, with increased aroma, reduced irritancy, and

related enzymes (PPO), and polyphenol synthase (PAL) 
were signicantly higher than those in unfermented 
tobacco leaves. Among the treatments, cigar tobacco 
leaves treated with 0.8% malic acid + 1.5% glucose yielded

Abstract
This study explored the eects of an acidic fermentation environment on the quality of cigar tobacco leaves 
using air-cured Dexue 1 tobacco leaves as the raw material. Malic acid was used as a pH regulator and three 
concentrations were screened to identify an optimal level for co-fermentation with 1.5% glucose. The potential 
mechanisms by which acidic fermentation reduces tobacco leaf irritancy were also analyzed. Fermentation under 
acidic conditions led to a more balanced chemical composition and to reduced irritancy. In the T2 (0.8% malic 
acid) and T3 (0.8% malic acid + 1.5% glucose) treatment groups, free nicotine proportion decreased by 37.52% and 
46.98%, respectively, compared to the unfermented treatment (CK). Enzymatic activities of carbon- and nitrogen-
metabolizing enzymes (alpha-amylase, neutral protease), a browning-related enzyme (polyphenol oxidase), and a 
polyphenol synthesis enzyme (phenylalanine ammonia lyase) were signicantly higher in fermented tobacco leaves 
than in unfermented ones. Microbial abundance and diversity were also substantially elevated post-fermentation. 
Dominant bacterial genera included Staphylococcus, Pantoea, Ralstonia, Pseudomonas, and Bacillus. Staphylococcus 
exhibited a signicantly positive correlation with protein and nicotine content, as well as a signicant or highly 
signicant negative correlation with total sugar, amino acids, and NH
3
 content. Metabolomic analysis revealed that 
the primary enriched metabolic pathways were the citrate cycle and phenylalanine metabolism. Staphylococcus 
was positively correlated with acetyl-CoA, isocitrate, and trans-2-hydroxycinnamic acid levels, whereas Bacillus was 
signicantly positively correlated with cis-aconitate and citrate. Under acidic conditions, N exists as NH
4
+
, which is 
more stable and less likely to volatilize during combustion, thus reducing NH
3
 release. Moreover, the proportion of

Introduction
Compared with ue-cured tobacco, cigars are uniquely 
hand-made from tobacco leaves that undergo fermenta-
tion and aging. ey are characterized by a richer and 
sweeter aroma, higher physiological strength, and a dis-
tinct style, and their market is rapidly expanding (Zong et 
al. 2023). After air-curing, cigar tobacco leaves undergo 
a specialized fermentation process that enhances their 
quality and usability. e fermentation of cigar tobacco 
leaves is a process in which microorganisms use nutrients 
of the tobacco leaves themselves to grow, metabolize, and 
transform under suitable conditions. It is an important 
link from agricultural raw materials to cigar products (Li 
et al. 2020a, b). Microorganisms produce small-molecule 
metabolites during fermentation by secreting enzymes 
that break down and employ organic substrates such as 
sugars, proteins, and lipids, thereby supporting their 
own growth and reproduction (Liu et al. 2021). After fer-
mentation, tobacco leaves exhibit obvious alterations in 
terms of physicochemical properties; aroma components 
are increased, sensory quality is improved, and these 
changes ultimately shape the unique stylistic features of 
cigars (Zheng et al. 2022). erefore, fermentation is a 
key step in improving the quality of cigar tobacco leaves 
(Zhou et al. 2020). Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, 
Sphingomonas, Pantomonas, and Methylobacterium are 
the primary bacterial genera involved in the fermentation 
of cigar leaves. For instance, Pseudomonas can degrade 
nicotine during fermentation (Wang et al. 2023a, b); sev-
eral Chryseobacterium strains exhibit protease activity, 
enabling them to hydrolyze proteins and produce amino 
acids (Wang et al. 2024), and Bacillus can break-down 
large molecules such as lignin and carotene by secreting 
relevant enzymes, thus generating small aromatic com-
pounds (Maldonado-Robledo et al. 2003). ese micro-
organisms play important roles in shaping the chemical 
composition, improving the quality, and contributing to 
the formation of benecial substances in cigar tobacco 
leaves.
Addition of organic acids to the culture medium aects 
the microbial utilization of carbon sources. For example, 
a previous study showed that adding moderate amounts 
of organic acids during the fermentation of cassava foli-
age silage signicantly alters the bacterial community 
structure. Using malic or citric acid in combination with 
Lactobacillus plantarum increased the abundance of 
potentially benecial microorganism such as Cellulosi-
microbium, Hyphomicrobium, and Oceanobacillus (Li 
et al. 2020a, b). Lv et al. demonstrated that citric acid 
addition minimizes the loss of dry matter and reduces 
the NH
4
+
N content during the fermentation of Amo-
mum villosum silage. is was achieved by inhibiting the 
growth of harmful bacteria such as Enterobacter, Esche-
richia-Shigella, and Pantoea, thereby improving overall 
fermentation quality (Lv et al. 2020). Furthermore, spray-
ing tobacco leaves with an appropriate concentration of 
glucose or citric acid before curing is reported to help 
reduce irritation and unpleasant odors, such as spiciness 
and bitterness (Blum 2005). ese ndings revealed that 
the addition of organic acids or sugar-based compounds 
can reduce smoke irritancy, while also regulating sensory 
quality.
L-malic acid is a naturally occurring organic acid that 
eectively preserves fruit acidity and is considered to 
have a superior taste compared to citric acid. It is also an 
important organic acid produced during human metab-
olism and serves as a key intermediate in the tricar-
boxylic acid (TCA) cycle. L-malic acid can enhance the 
metabolic activity of related microorganisms by promot-
ing reactions within metabolic pathways and has been 
widely used in the food industry for this reason (Wu et al. 
2022). Preliminary tests showed that fermentation under 
acidic conditions signicantly reduces the irritancy of 
cigar tobacco leaves. As pH represents a critical regula-
tory factor in this process, two specic hypotheses have 
been proposed. First, nicotine forms are closely corre-
lated with pH value, and the proportion of free nicotine 
decreases with a decline in pH. Second, under acidic con-
ditions, nitrogen is primarily stabilized in its protonated 
form (NH
4

tilize as NH during combustion. ese two mechanisms 
are considered the primary contributors to the reduction 
in cigar tobacco leaf irritancy. To explore this, malic acid 
was used as a pH-regulating agent to study how a lower 
fermentation pH aects the physiological characteristics, 
microbial diversity, and metabolite enrichment path-
ways of cigar tobacco leaves. e aim was to elucidate the

Discussion
During fermentation, the chemical composition of 
tobacco leaves is closely related to microbial activity. 
After the addition of malic acid, the water-soluble sugar 
content of the tobacco leaves increases, likely owing to 
a pH reduction, which partially inhibits the growth of 
alkaline-favoring microbes, potentially limiting respira-
tion and microbial proliferation (Ye et al. 2023). Malic 
acid is an intermediate product in several metabolic 
pathways, such as the TCA cycle, and it may promote 
bacterial growth by enhancing microbial metabolic activ-
ity through its involvement in key reactions, which is 
consistent with the enrichment of carbohydrate metabo-
lism pathways observed in this study (Skorokhodova et 
al. 2022). Previous studies have shown that co-fermen-
tation with malic acid and glucose reduces impurities in 
tobacco leaves, decreases irritancy, increases sweetness, 
and improves overall sensory quality. ese eects may 
be primarily associated with two mechanisms. First, the 
acidic substances derived from malic acid and its metab-
olites can combine with nicotine to form nicotine salts. 
is converts nicotine from its free-base form to a bound 
state, which may reduce its release into smoke and low-
ering smoke irritancy, while also modulating nicotine 
absorption (Blum 2005). e ndings in our study are

and diversity than fungal communities, suggesting that

relative abundances of Pantoea, Ralstonia, and Bacillus 
increased, indicating that these strains can adapt to the

ment of tobacco leaves.
Microorganisms may inuence fermentation indirectly, 
primarily through the expression of functional genes that 
aect the biosynthesis and degradation of key enzymes, 
thereby regulating metabolic processes (Ouyang et al. 
2018; Zhang et al. 2023). Based on the results of corre-
lation analysis and PICRUSt2 functional predictions, 
an association existed between dierent microbial taxa 
and the chemical components of tobacco leaves. Nota-
bly, PICRUSt2 is a predictive tool that infers microbial 
functional potential based on 16S rRNA gene sequence 
data, and its predictions do not reect the actual func-
tional activity of microorganisms; thus, the functional 
associations inferred in this study require further veri-
cation through experiments. Bacillus has been reported 
to synthesize various hydrolases such as glucoamylase 
and protease (Huang et al. 2017). Given the increased 
relative abundance of Bacillus in fermented leaves along-
side decreased protein and elevated amino acid levels, 
we hypothesize that members of this genus may con-
tribute to protein hydrolysis and amino acid accumula-
tion, which could improve the taste characteristics of 
tobacco leaves (Liu et al. 2021). Staphylococcus exhibited 
a signicant or highly signicant positive correlation 
with the contents of protein, nicotine, and ammonium 
nitrogen in cigar tobacco leaves. We speculate that the 
potential reasons may be as follows: Staphylococcus 
can secrete proteases to degrade tobacco leaf proteins, 
thereby obtaining amino acids as nitrogen and energy 
sources to sustain its growth (Zhang et al. 2024); mean-
while, the deamination of amino acids promotes ammo-
nium nitrogen accumulation, and some functional strains 
may mediate nicotine transformation through nicotine 
oxidase to further employ it as a carbon and nitrogen 
source (Yao et al. 2025); Additionally, the high-temper-
ature, micro-oxic conditions during mid-fermentation 
could favor Staphylococcus proliferation and enhance the 
activity of enzymes involved in protein degradation and 
nicotine transformation (Zhang et al. 2024). Notably, this 
correlation likely reects a metabolic association rather 
than a direct causal relationship and may be inuenced 
by factors such as metabolic heterogeneity among strains 
within the genus Staphylococcus and mediation by fer-
mentation environmental factors. e specic mecha-
nism of action requires further clarication through pure 
culture experiments, functional gene verication, and 
other approaches. Aspergillus has been conrmed to be 
involved in sugar and protein degradation, and in the 
synthesis of avor-related compounds in tobacco (Mu 
et al. 2020). Additionally, it can create an air-isolation 
eect and inhibit harmful microorganisms, suggesting 
a positive role in tobacco quality formation. e afore-
mentioned microbial taxa do not act in isolation during 
fermentation; rather, they likely regulate leaf quality syn-
ergistically through complex community interaction net-
works (Gralka et al. 2020; Ma et al. 2021).
During the fermentation process, metabolite-enriched 
pathways were primarily the citrate cycle and phenylala-
nine metabolism. Notably, intermediates of carbohydrate 
metabolism can serve as precursors for the biosynthesis 
of aromatic amino acids (Wang et al. 2023a, b). In addi-
tion, the Maillard reaction involving amino acids and 
reducing sugars constitutes a crucial pathway for the 
formation of aroma-forming substances in tobacco and 
is directly correlated with the sensory quality of tobacco 
leaves (Ren et al. 2023). In the present study, citric acid 
was upregulated in the citrate cycle. We hypothesize 
that this is associated with the catalytic action of citrate 
synthase, a key enzyme that mediates the initial reaction 
of the citrate cycle. Changes in its activity may regulate 
the allocation of carbon ux into the cycle pathway and 
enhance overall metabolic activity (Kumar et al. 2023). 
is hypothesis can be further veried by measuring 
the activities of related metabolic enzymes. e prolif-
eration of most microorganisms relies on the endogenous 
organic substances in tobacco leaves. ese microor-
ganisms likely participate in the degradation of carbon-
containing compounds and proteins during tobacco leaf 
fermentation to maintain their own growth and metabo-
lism, thereby promoting the enrichment of metabolites in 
carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism pathways.
Conclusions
e chemical components of cigar tobacco leaves in

*AMB Express* (2026)16:41https://doi.org/10.1186/s13568-026-02034-4## AbstractThis study explored the effects of an acidic fermentation environment on the quality of cigar tobacco leaves using air-cured “Dexue1” tobacco leaves as the raw material. Malic acid was used as a pH regulator and three concentrations were screened to identify an optimal level for co-fermentation with1.5% glucose. The potential mechanisms by which acidic fermentation reduces tobacco leaf irritancy were also analyzed. Fermentation under acidic conditions led to a more balanced chemical composition and to reduced irritancy. In the T2 (0.8% malic acid) and T3 (0.8% malic acid +1.5% glucose) treatment groups, free nicotine proportion decreased by37.52% and46.98%, respectively, compared to the unfermented treatment (CK). Enzymatic activities of carbon- and nitrogen-metabolizing enzymes (alpha-amylase, neutral protease), a browning-related enzyme (polyphenol oxidase), and a polyphenol synthesis enzyme (phenylalanine ammonia lyase) were significantly higher in fermented tobacco leaves than in unfermented ones. Microbial abundance and diversity were also substantially elevated post-fermentation. Dominant bacterial genera included *Staphylococcus*, *Pantoea*, *Ralstonia*, *Pseudomonas*, and *Bacillus*. *Staphylococcus* exhibited a significantly positive correlation with protein and nicotine content, as well as a significant or highly significant negative correlation with total sugar, amino acids, and NH₃ content. Metabolomic analysis revealed that the primary enriched metabolic pathways were the citrate cycle and phenylalanine metabolism. *Staphylococcus* was positively correlated with acetyl-CoA, isocitrate, and trans-2-hydroxycinnamic acid levels, whereas *Bacillus* was significantly positively correlated with cis-aconitate and citrate. Under acidic conditions, N exists as NH₄⁺, which is more stable and less likely to volatilize during combustion, thus reducing NH₃ release. Moreover, the proportion of free nicotine decreased as pH decreased. Collectively, these factors reduced the irritancy of cigar tobacco leaves fermented under acidic conditions.

**Keywords**: Acidic fermentation, Cigar tobacco leaves, Microbial diversity, Tobacco quality, Metabolite## IntroductionCompared with flue-cured tobacco, cigars are uniquely hand-made from tobacco leaves that undergo fermentation and aging. They are characterized by a richer and sweeter aroma, higher physiological strength, and a distinct style, and their market is rapidly expanding (Zong et al.2023). After air-curing, cigar tobacco leaves undergo a specialized fermentation process that enhances their quality and usability. The fermentation of cigar tobacco leaves is a process in which microorganisms use nutrients of the tobacco leaves themselves to grow, metabolize, and transform under suitable conditions. It is an important link from agricultural raw materials to cigar products (Li et al.2020a, b). Microorganisms produce small-molecule metabolites during fermentation by secreting enzymes that break down and employ organic substrates such as sugars, proteins, and lipids, thereby supporting their own growth and reproduction (Liu et al.2021). After fermentation, tobacco leaves exhibit obvious alterations in terms of physicochemical properties; aroma components are increased, sensory quality is improved, and these changes ultimately shape the unique stylistic features of cigars (Zheng et al.2022). Therefore, fermentation is a key step in improving the quality of cigar tobacco leaves (Zhou et al.2020). *Bacillus*, *Pseudomonas*, *Enterobacter*, *Sphingomonas*, *Pantomonas*, and *Methylobacterium* are the primary bacterial genera involved in the fermentation of cigar leaves. For instance, *Pseudomonas* can degrade nicotine during fermentation (Wang et al.2023a, b); several *Chryseobacterium* strains exhibit protease activity, enabling them to hydrolyze proteins and produce amino acids (Wang et al.2024), and *Bacillus* can break-down large molecules such as lignin and carotene by secreting relevant enzymes, thus generating small aromatic compounds (Maldonado-Robledo et al.2003). These microorganisms play important roles in shaping the chemical composition, improving the quality, and contributing to the formation of beneficial substances in cigar tobacco leaves.

Addition of organic acids to the culture medium affects the microbial utilization of carbon sources. For example, a previous study showed that adding moderate amounts of organic acids during the fermentation of cassava foliage silage significantly alters the bacterial community structure. Using malic or citric acid in combination with *Lactobacillus plantarum* increased the abundance of potentially beneficial microorganism such as *Cellulosimicrobium*, *Hyphomicrobium*, and *Oceanobacillus* (Li et al.2020a, b). Lv et al. demonstrated that citric acid addition minimizes the loss of dry matter and reduces the NH₄⁺–N content during the fermentation of *Amomum villosum* silage. This was achieved by inhibiting the growth of harmful bacteria such as *Enterobacter*, *Escherichia-Shigella*, and *Pantoea*, thereby improving overall fermentation quality (Lv et al.2020). Furthermore, spraying tobacco leaves with an appropriate concentration of glucose or citric acid before curing is reported to help reduce irritation and unpleasant odors, such as spiciness and bitterness (Blum2005). These findings revealed that the addition of organic acids or sugar-based compounds can reduce smoke irritancy, while also regulating sensory quality.

L-malic acid is a naturally occurring organic acid that effectively preserves fruit acidity and is considered to have a superior taste compared to citric acid. It is also an important organic acid produced during human metabolism and serves as a key intermediate in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. L-malic acid can enhance the metabolic activity of related microorganisms by promoting reactions within metabolic pathways and has been widely used in the food industry for this reason (Wu et al.2022). Preliminary tests showed that fermentation under acidic conditions significantly reduces the irritancy of cigar tobacco leaves. As pH represents a critical regulatory factor in this process, two specific hypotheses have been proposed. First, nicotine forms are closely correlated with pH value, and the proportion of free nicotine decreases with a decline in pH. Second, under acidic conditions, nitrogen is primarily stabilized in its protonated form (NH₄⁺), which is more stable and less likely to volatilize as NH₃ during combustion. These two mechanisms are considered the primary contributors to the reduction in cigar tobacco leaf irritancy. To explore this, malic acid was used as a pH-regulating agent to study how a lower fermentation pH affects the physiological characteristics, microbial diversity, and metabolite enrichment pathways of cigar tobacco leaves. The aim was to elucidate the mechanism by which acidic conditions reduce irritancy and establish a theoretical foundation for improving the quality of cigar fermentation.

## Materials and Methods### Experimental MaterialsThe experimental materials comprised medium, second-grade cigar wrapper leaves of uniform quality after air-curing, with a moisture content of approximately28%. These were obtained in2024 from the traditional cigar variety “Dexue1” provided by the Sichuan Tobacco Company (Sichuan, China).

### Experimental Design#### Screening for Optimal Malic Acid ConcentrationMalic acid was used at concentrations of0.4%,0.8%, and1.2%, designated as P1, P2, and P3, respectively. The unfermented samples served as the control (CK). After moisture regain,500 g of tobacco leaves was evenly sprayed with the respective malic acid solutions, allowed to stand for10 min, and then sealed in self-sealing bags. Fermentation was conducted for7 d under controlled indoor conditions (temperature,40 °C; relative humidity,80%). Nicotine, protein, total nitrogen, and reducing sugar content, as well as sensory quality, were analyzed for each treatment. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to determine the optimal concentration of malic acid.

#### Synergistic Fermentation of Malic Acid and GlucoseThe samples were organized into four treatment groups: unfermented (CK), distilled water (T1),0.8% malic acid (T2), and0.8% malic acid +1.5% glucose (T3), with three replicates per treatment. After moisture regain,1 kg of tobacco leaves per treatment was uniformly spray-misted with the respective solutions. Samples were allowed to stand for10 min and then sealed in self-sealing bags. Fermentation was performed for28 d under controlled indoor conditions (temperature,40 °C; relative humidity,80%). After fermentation,20 g of tobacco leaves was rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C for subsequent enzyme activity, amino acid content, microbial diversity, and metabolomic analyses. A100 g portion of tobacco leaves was dried in an oven at60 °C for4 h, ground, and passed through a0.25 mm mesh sieve (60 mesh) for the analysis of conventional chemical components and free nicotine content. An additional200 g of tobacco leaves was manually rolled into cigars of uniform specifications for sensory quality evaluation. For metabolomics determination and sensory quality evaluations, six biological replicates were performed per treatment, whereas three biological replicates were used for all other measurements. Therefore, all analytical measurements and sensory quality evaluations were performed on subsamples derived from the same batch of fermented tobacco leaves, thus ensuring consistency and comparability across all experimental results.

### Measurement Methods#### Chemical CompositionTotal sugar and reducing sugar contents were determined in accordance with YC/T159–2019 using a continuous flow analyzer (AA3; BRAN&LU-EBBE, Germany). Protein content was measured based on YC/T249–2008, and total nitrogen content was determined according to YC/T161–2002. Nicotine content was determined based on YC/T559–2018 using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). The pH of the cigar leaves was measured using an acidometer (PB-10; Sartorius, Göttingen, Germany) according to YC/T222–2007. NH₄⁺-N content was quantified using the phenol-sodium hypochlorite colorimetric method and a microplate reader (Synergy H1; Biotek, Winooski, VT, USA). NH₃ concentration was measured using an ammonia detector (EDKORS X-1, China).

#### Amino Acid ContentAmino acid content was determined using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Briefly,1 mL of ultrapure water was added to0.05 g of the ground tobacco sample in a microcentrifuge tube. After overnight extraction, the supernatant (200 µL) and an amino acid standard solution (200 µL) were transferred to1.5 mL tubes. Next, an N-leucine internal standard solution (20 µL), triethylamine acetonitrile solution (pH >7) (200 µL), and100% phenyl isothiocyanate acetonitrile solution were added and incubated at25 °C for1 h. After incubation, N-Hexane (400 µL) was added, and the solution was incubated for an additional10 min. The final solution was filtered and analyzed using a Rigol L3000 HPLC system (Beijing, China).

#### Free Nicotine ContentOne gram of tobacco sample (accurate to0.0001 g) was placed in a150 mL stoppered conical flask. Subsequently,30 mL of CO₂-free distilled water, adjusted to pH7.00 with0.01 mol/L NaOH, was added. The mixture was shaken and extracted at room temperature for30 min, then filtered. Next,15 mL of the filtrate was transferred to a250 mL separating funnel and extracted twice with200 mL of trichloromethane (containing internal standard n-heptadecane). The organic phases were combined for GC analysis. A nicotine standard sample was prepared in a standard solution, and GC analysis was performed to determine the relative retention time of the nicotine peak, which was then compared with the relative retention time of the corresponding peak in the tobacco sample. The internal standard curve method was used to quantitatively analyze nicotine content. The GC conditions were as follows: chromatographic column, DB-5 quartz capillary column; injection port temperature,250 °C; column flow rate,1.0 mL/min; injection volume,1.0 µL; and split ratio,10:1. The oven temperature program was as follows:100 °C for2 min, increased at10 °C/min to200 °C, then ramped at20 °C/min to280 °C, and held for5 min.

#### Enzymatic Activity MeasurementsTobacco polyphenol oxidase (PPO), phenylalanine ammonia lyase (PAL), alpha-amylase (α-AL), and neutral protease (NP) activities were measured using reagent kits (Suzhou Keming Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Jiangsu, China).

#### Microbial Diversity AnalysisMicrobial DNA was extracted using a HiPure Soil DNA Kit (Magen, Guangzhou, China). The V5–V7 region of16S rDNA was amplified using the following specific barcoded PCR primers:799F (5′-AACMGGATTAGATACCCKG-3′) and1193R (5′-ACGTCATCCCCACCTTCC-3′). In addition, the fungal amplification primers used were ITS1F (5′-CTTGGTCATTTAGAGGAAGTAA-3′) and ITS2 (5′-GCTGCGTTCTTCATCGATGC-3′). The target region of ribosomal RNA was amplified using PCR. The amplification products were quantified using a QuantiFluor™ fluorometer (Promega, Madison, WI, USA), followed by library construction and sequencing using an Illumina PE250 platform (San Diego, CA, USA). The sequencing data were spliced using FLASH (v.1.2.7) (Magoc and Salzberg2011) to obtain raw reads, which were then filtered and processed using Fastp software (Bokulich et al.2013). The Uparse algorithm (Edgar2013) was used for clustering analysis, and sequences were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) based on97% similarity. The OTU sequences were then annotated and aligned with the species. Bacterial OTUs were annotated using the Mothur method and the SILVA138 SSU rRNA database. Fungal OTUs were annotated and analyzed using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) method in Quantitative Insights Into Microbial Ecology (QIIME) software (v.1.9.1) and the Unite (v.8.2) database (Edgar2004; Wang et al.2007).

#### Metabolomic AnalysisThe samples were separated using an Agilent1290 Infinity LC Ultra (U)HPLC (hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography, HILIC) system (Santa Clara, CA, USA) at a column temperature of25 °C, flow rate of0.5 mL/min, and injection volume of2 µL. Samples were loaded onto a Hypersil Gold column (100 mm ×2.1 mm,1.9 µm) using a linear gradient deliver over17 min (flow rate:0.2 mL/min). For positive polarity mode,0.1% FA in water was used as eluent A, and methanol was used as eluent B. For negative polarity mode,5 mM ammonium acetate (pH9.0) was used as eluent A, and methanol was used as eluent B. The solvent gradient program was as follows:2% B for1.5 min;2%–100% B over12.0 min;100% B for14.0 min;100%–2% B over14.1 min; and2% B for17 min. A Triple TOF6600 Quantity Spectrometer (AB SCIEX, Framingham, MA, USA) was used for high-resolution spectrometry. Differential metabolites between groups were screened using orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA), based on variable importance in projection values and P-values from Student’s t-tests. Metabolite levels were considered significantly different when the variable importance in projection was ≥1 and P <0.05. Each treatment was conducted using six biological replicates to ensure biological universality and reliability of the experimental results.

#### Sensory Quality EvaluationAfter fermentation, the tobacco leaves were manually rolled into single-blend cigar samples with a length of90 mm and diameter of9.5 mm. These samples were then placed in a constant temperature and humidity chamber (Binder KBF240, Germany), maintained at18 °C and68% relative humidity for30 d to equilibrate the moisture content. Sensory quality evaluation was conducted by a panel of six certified professional sensory panelists (men, aged40–50 years), among whom three were from the National Research Base of Crop Cultivation Physiology and Biochemistry, Henan Agricultural University, and three were from Sichuan Tobacco Industry Co., Ltd. The panelists performed independent scoring on sensory attributes, including aroma quality, aroma quantity, aftertaste, offensive odor, sweetness, irritancy, combustibility, cigarette ash, in accordance with the YC/T415–2011 Sensory Evaluation Methods for Tobacco Processing and using a nine-point system. For statistical analysis of the sensory scores, the mean score of the six panelists was first calculated for each treatment. Subsequently, the least significant difference test (P <0.05) was conducted to determine the significant differences in sensory quality among the different treatments.

### Data Processing and AnalysisStatistical analysis was performed using Excel2011 (Microsoft, Redmond, WA, USA). Charts were created using Origin2021 (OriginLab, Northampton, MA, USA), and statistical significance testing (P <0.05) was assessed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) test using SPSS22.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). PCA of the selected indicators was conducted using SPSS22.0. Based on the classified OTUs, bacterial and fungal alpha diversity was calculated using QIIME software (Sobs, Ace, Chao, Simpson, and Shannon indices) (Caporaso et al.2010). Differential microbiological clusters and representative taxa were analyzed using linear discriminant analysis (LDA) effect size (LEfSe) with LDA thresholds of3.5 for bacteria and2.5 for fungi (Segata et al.2011). PCA and OPLS-DA were conducted using Rstudio and Ropls packages (Wang et al.2007). Species abundance Circos plots were generated using Circos software (Krzywinski et al.2009). The Mantel test was conducted using OmicShare Tools, and correlation analysis was performed using Cytoscape software.

## Results### Selection of Optimal Malic Acid ConcentrationTo determine the optimal malic acid concentration, PCA was used to evaluate ten related indicators, including chemical composition and sensory quality. The factor loadings of the ten indicators on the principal components were analyzed, and their eigenvalues and contributions were calculated (Table S1).
